proposals.title: Cap anytime search well under the stated limit and make the cap global
proposals.trigger: The solution uses an anytime loop (simulated annealing, beam, repeated restarts) that runs until a self-measured deadline derived from the problem's stated execution time limit, and the public judge has so far returned ACCEPTED.
procedure: Derive the internal deadline as a fixed fraction of the stated limit (leave a clear margin), not as the limit minus a few milliseconds; the grading machine may be slower than the public one.

Measure elapsed time from process start with a single monotonic clock and check it inside every inner loop that can run long, including construction, repair and output phases — not only the main optimization loop.
Make the worst case bounded independently of input: any per-iteration cost that grows with input size must be divided out of the iteration budget so the largest instances still finish.
After each round, scale the margin by observed headroom only downward, never upward: if any case's score pattern suggests near-limit behaviour, shrink the internal deadline rather than extending it.
Prefer winning score by better moves per unit time over winning it by consuming more wall-clock; if a change only helps because it runs longer, reject it.
Keep a guaranteed-valid fallback answer written before the search begins so an early abort still emits legal output.
successSignals: Every submitted round returns ACCEPTED and the final graded verdict matches the public verdict.
Score improvements across rounds come from algorithmic changes while measured runtime stays flat and below the self-imposed cap.
failureSignals: Any round's verdict changes to TIME_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, or the final verdict differs from the public verdicts.
The internal deadline equals or nearly equals the stated limit, or long phases exist with no clock check.
recovery: Immediately resubmit the current best variant with the internal deadline reduced substantially and clock checks added to every unbounded loop, before attempting any further quality improvement.
invariants: Never set the internal deadline to the full stated limit.
Legal output must be producible at any abort point.

proposals.title: Treat the best measured variant as the base; revert instead of stacking onto a regression
proposals.trigger: A submission round returns an aggregate score worse than the best aggregate seen so far in this episode, and submission rounds remain.
procedure: Keep the exact source of the best-scoring variant so far; treat it, not the most recent variant, as the base for the next edit.
When the latest round regressed, discard the regressing change and re-derive the next edit from the stored best base.
Make one conceptually isolated change per round so each round's score difference attributes to that change.
Use the per-case score breakdown already returned to decide where to edit: target the cases that are weakest relative to the best base, not uniform rewrites.
Resist monotone code growth; if a change adds substantial code without an aggregate gain over the best base, remove it.
Reserve the last round to resubmit the stored best base verbatim if no later variant has beaten it.
successSignals: Aggregate score is non-decreasing across the second half of the episode and the final submission equals or beats the episode's best.
Code size plateaus while score still improves.
failureSignals: Two or more consecutive rounds below the best-so-far aggregate while code size keeps growing.
Final submission scores below a variant submitted earlier in the same episode.
recovery: Resubmit the stored best variant unchanged to re-anchor, then resume with a single small edit.
invariants: Never build the next revision on top of a variant that scored worse than the stored best.
Exactly one isolated change per round.
